questions.stem: A 36 year old woman who smokes 15 cigarettes a day has 3 months of painful swelling of her knuckles, the middle joints of her fingers and both wrists. She is stiff for 90 minutes each morning. The joints at the ends of her fingers are normal. She has no rash, nail changes or mouth ulcers.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Symmetrical polyarthritis of the MCPs, PIPs and wrists sparing the DIPs, with morning stiffness over an hour, in a smoker is RA.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.

clues: knuckles, the middle joints of her fingers and both wrists
ends of her fingers are normal
steps.x: **Symmetrical** MCP + PIP + wrist, **DIPs spared**, stiffness **over 1 hour**. Smoking is a risk factor.

elim: An acute monoarthritis, not a 3 month symmetrical polyarthritis.
Affects the DIP joints and thumb base, with short morning stiffness.
Often involves the DIP joints with nail pitting and psoriasis.
Non-erosive arthralgia with rash, mouth ulcers and serositis.

steps.x: **D. Rheumatoid arthritis.** RA = symmetrical small joint polyarthritis sparing the DIPs, morning stiffness over 1 hour.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman has a 5 month history of symmetrical hand pain and swelling with morning stiffness for over an hour. Her anti-CCP antibodies are strongly positive. A medical student examining her hands is asked which joints would typically be unaffected in her condition.
questions.q: Which joints are most likely to be spared?
questions.e: RA characteristically spares the DIP joints; DIP involvement suggests osteoarthritis or psoriatic arthritis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which joints are most likely to be spared? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.
Symmetrical polyarthritis + **anti-CCP positive** = RA. Which small joints does RA leave alone?

elim: The commonest site of RA synovitis.
Often involved in RA, causing hammer toes.
Typically involved in RA.
Typically involved in RA.

steps.x: **A. Distal interphalangeal joints.** RA spares the DIPs; OA and psoriatic arthritis hit them.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman has had rheumatoid arthritis for 18 years. Her right ring finger is fixed with the middle joint bent and the joint at the tip pushed back straight. She can no longer straighten the middle joint actively.
questions.q: Which is the most likely deformity?
questions.e: Boutonnière deformity is a flexed PIP with a hyperextended DIP; swan neck is the reverse.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely deformity? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.
**PIP flexed, DIP hyperextended** in long-standing RA.

elim: Thickened palmar fascia flexing the MCP joint, with a palpable cord.
Flexed DIP after extensor tendon injury at the tip; the PIP is normal.
The reverse: hyperextended PIP with a flexed DIP.
The finger locks in flexion and clicks free.

steps.x: **A. Boutonnière deformity.** Boutonnière = PIP flexed, DIP hyperextended. Swan neck = PIP hyperextended, DIP flexed.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man has had seropositive rheumatoid arthritis for 25 years. When he rests his hands on the table, his fingers drift towards the little finger side at the knuckles. His thumb is bent at the MCP joint and pushed back at the interphalangeal joint.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding at his MCP joints?
questions.e: Long-standing RA causes ulnar deviation at the MCP joints, often with a Z-thumb deformity.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding at his MCP joints? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.

clues: fingers drift towards the little finger side
pushed back at the interphalangeal joint
steps.x: Fingers drift to the **little finger (ulnar) side** + a **Z-thumb** in long-standing RA.

elim: Bony swellings of the PIP joints in osteoarthritis.
Bony swellings of the DIP joints in osteoarthritis.
The fingers drift the OTHER way in RA.
Arthritis mutilans of psoriatic arthritis.

steps.x: **E. Ulnar deviation.** RA hand: ulnar deviation, Z-thumb, swan neck, boutonnière.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman with long-standing seropositive rheumatoid arthritis has had two chest infections this winter. She has leg ulcers and her spleen is palpable 4 cm below the costal margin. She is not taking methotrexate or any other DMARD. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Felty's syndrome is RA with splenomegaly and neutropenia, raising the risk of bacterial infection.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.
RA + **splenomegaly** + **neutropenia** (off DMARDs) + recurrent infections.

elim: Blasts on the film with anaemia and thrombocytopenia.
Lung nodules in RA with dust exposure, not splenomegaly.
She takes no DMARDs.
Not with long-standing erosive seropositive RA and a large spleen.

steps.x: **D. Felty's syndrome.** Felty's = RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man with rheumatoid arthritis worked as a coal miner for 25 years and smoked for 30 years. He has a mild cough. His temperature is 36.9°C and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows several well-defined round nodules, 1 to 3 cm, in both lungs.

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Multiple well-defined round nodules in both lungs.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Caplan syndrome is rheumatoid pneumoconiosis: intrapulmonary nodules in RA with coal, silica or asbestos dust exposure and smoking.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.
RA + **coal dust** + smoking + **multiple lung nodules**.

elim: RA with splenomegaly and neutropenia, not lung nodules.
Possible, but his RA plus coal dust exposure points to rheumatoid pneumoconiosis.
Tiny 1 to 3 mm nodules with fever and weight loss.
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy rather than discrete nodules.

steps.x: **A. Caplan syndrome.** Caplan = RA + dust exposure + lung nodules.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has a 2 day history of a red patch on the white of her left eye. It feels gritty but is not painful, and her vision is normal. There is no discharge. The redness is in one sector and the vessels move when gently pressed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Episcleritis in RA is gritty but not painful with normal vision; scleritis is painful.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.
RA eye that is **gritty, painless**, with normal vision and mobile vessels.

elim: Severe pain, haloes and reduced vision.
Painful with photophobia and blurred vision; linked to spondyloarthropathy.
Diffuse redness with sticky discharge.
Severe, deep boring PAIN, sometimes with reduced vision.

steps.x: **D. Episcleritis.** RA eyes: episcleritis (gritty, painless) vs scleritis (painful).

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has pain in the balls of both feet, like walking on pebbles. Squeezing across her forefoot is painful. Her second to fourth toes are bent at the middle joint and pushed up at the base, and she has calluses under the metatarsal heads.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her toe deformities?
o: MTP joint synovitis causing hammer toes
questions.e: RA commonly involves the MTP joints of the feet, causing hammer toe deformities; forefoot squeeze tenderness is the clue.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of her toe deformities? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.

clues: Squeezing across her forefoot is painful
steps.x: RA + **MTP squeeze tenderness** + toes bent at the PIP = **hammer toes** from MTP synovitis.

elim: Painless destruction in a numb diabetic foot.
Chalky deposits, usually over the first MTP.
Burning between the third and fourth toes, without deformity.
Heel pain on first standing.

steps.x: **D. MTP joint synovitis causing hammer toes.** RA feet: MTP synovitis and hammer toes; always examine the feet.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis, well controlled on methotrexate, has 5 days of worsening pain and swelling in both wrists, several MCP joints and both knees. She is stiff for 3 hours each morning and feels feverish and unwell. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An acute RA flare causes worsening joint pain with inflammatory stiffness, fever and malaise across many joints.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.

clues: worsening pain and swelling in both wrists, several MCP joints and both knees
steps.x: Many **symmetrical** joints worse at once + long stiffness + low-grade fever and malaise in known RA.

elim: Usually one acutely painful joint, not a symmetrical polyarthritis.
Causes cough and breathlessness, not joint swelling.
Usually a single knee or wrist in an older person.
Usually ONE hot joint with high fever; she has many symmetrical joints and a low-grade fever.

steps.x: **A. Acute flare of rheumatoid arthritis.** Polyarticular worsening + malaise in RA = flare; a single hot joint = think septic.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman is diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis after 4 months of symmetrical hand synovitis. She has firm, non-tender lumps over both elbows. She smokes and finds it hard to manage stairs. Her rheumatologist reviews her results to estimate her prognosis.
questions.q: Which result would most indicate a poor prognosis?
o: Positive antinuclear antibody at low titre
questions.e: Positive RF and anti-CCP (with nodules, smoking, insidious onset and poor function) indicate a poor prognosis; anti-CCP is linked to erosions.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which result would most indicate a poor prognosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.

clues: firm, non-tender lumps over both elbows
steps.x: She already has **nodules**, **smoking** and **poor function**. Which test result adds to these poor prognosis markers?

elim: A GOOD prognostic sign.
No erosions yet is reassuring.
Not a prognostic marker.
A non-specific finding.

steps.x: **D. Positive anti-CCP antibodies.** RA poor prognosis: nodules, RF and anti-CCP positive, smoking, HLA-DR4, poor function.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman has had seropositive rheumatoid arthritis for 15 years. She has 2 months of central chest tightness when walking uphill, relieved by rest within 5 minutes. She does not smoke. Her BP is 136/84 mmHg. A resting ECG is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her chest pain?
questions.e: RA raises the risk of ischaemic heart disease; exertional chest tightness relieved by rest is stable angina.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of her chest pain? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.
Exertional, relieved by rest = **angina**. Chronic RA inflammation accelerates atherosclerosis.

elim: Sharp, reproducible chest wall tenderness, not exertional.
Burning after meals or lying flat.
Sharp pain eased by sitting forward, with ECG changes.
Breathlessness with dullness, not exertional chest tightness relieved by rest.

steps.x: **C. Ischaemic heart disease.** RA increases cardiovascular risk: ischaemic heart disease is a key complication.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has 6 months of increasing breathlessness on exertion and ankle swelling. Her JVP is raised, the second heart sound is loud in the pulmonary area and her chest is clear. Echocardiography shows normal left ventricular function and an estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 58 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A loud P2, raised JVP, oedema and a high pulmonary artery pressure with normal LV function is pulmonary hypertension, a complication of RA.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.

clues: pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 58 mmHg
steps.x: **Loud P2** + right heart failure + **high PA pressure** with a normal LV.

elim: An ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids.
Lung nodules with dust exposure.
Kussmaul's sign and pericardial calcification, with normal pulmonary pressure.
Her left ventricle works normally and her chest is clear.

steps.x: **E. Pulmonary hypertension.** RA complications: pulmonary hypertension, IHD, effusion, atlantoaxial subluxation.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man has 4 months of swelling of the small joints of both hands. He is trying to decide with his GP whether it is inflammatory. He has no psoriasis and his nails are normal. His GP asks him how the joints feel at different times of day.
questions.q: Which description would most suggest rheumatoid arthritis?
o: Joints feel fine until he uses them, then ache by evening
Painless swelling only at the DIP joints
Sudden severe pain in one joint overnight
Swelling and stiffness that ease with use and worsen with rest
questions.e: Inflammatory swelling in RA improves with exertion and is worse at rest, with morning stiffness over an hour.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which description would most suggest rheumatoid arthritis? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.

clues: swelling of the small joints of both hands
steps.x: Inflammatory joints **loosen up with use** and stiffen with rest; mechanical joints do the reverse.

elim: A mechanical pattern, as in osteoarthritis.
Heberden's nodes of osteoarthritis.
Suggests gout.
Too short for inflammatory arthritis.

steps.x: **E. Swelling and stiffness that ease with use and worsen with rest.** RA: worse at rest, better with use, morning stiffness over 1 hour.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman has just been diagnosed with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis. She is HLA-DR4 positive, smokes 20 cigarettes a day, drinks 10 units of alcohol a week and has a BMI of 27. She asks what she can change to reduce her risk of severe disease.
questions.q: Which is the most important modifiable risk factor?
questions.e: Smoking is the key modifiable risk factor for RA and a poor prognostic marker; HLA-DR4 is a non-modifiable genetic risk.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most important modifiable risk factor? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.
Separate **modifiable** from fixed risks. HLA-DR4 and sex cannot change.

elim: Not a major RA risk factor at this level.
Weight affects joints but is not the key RA risk factor listed.
Not modifiable.
A genetic risk factor that cannot be changed.

steps.x: **E. Smoking.** RA risk factors: HLA-DR4 (genetic) and smoking (modifiable).

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has 3 months of painful swelling of both wrists and several knuckles, and pain under the balls of both feet when walking. He is stiff for 2 hours each morning. Squeezing across his knuckles and forefeet is painful. He has no psoriasis, back pain or recent infection.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A symmetrical polyarthritis of the wrists, MCPs and MTPs with prolonged morning stiffness is RA, which also affects men.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.

clues: pain under the balls of both feet
Squeezing across his knuckles and forefeet is painful
steps.x: **Symmetrical** hands + feet (MCP and MTP squeeze tenderness) + stiffness over an hour.

elim: Acute attacks in one joint at a time, not a 3 month symmetrical polyarthritis.
Shoulder and hip girdle stiffness without small joint synovitis.
Needs psoriasis or nail disease, often with DIP involvement.
An asymmetrical lower limb arthritis after infection.

steps.x: **E. Rheumatoid arthritis.** Positive MCP and MTP squeeze test + long morning stiffness = RA.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman has 3 months of symmetrical swelling of her MCP joints and wrists with 2 hours of morning stiffness. Her GP sends a full blood count, ESR, CRP and two antibody tests. She asks which antibody is most likely to be positive if she has rheumatoid arthritis.
questions.q: Which is the most sensitive marker?
questions.e: First-line bloods in RA include RF and anti-CCP; RF is the most sensitive, anti-CCP the most specific.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most sensitive marker? It wants a test (or a test result). Decide which test, and why, before reading the options.

clues: symmetrical swelling of her MCP joints and wrists
which antibody is most likely to be positive
steps.x: 'Most likely to be positive' = **sensitivity**. The two RA antibodies: RF (sensitive) and anti-CCP (specific).

elim: Specific for lupus.
Seen in polymyositis with lung disease.
Seen in Sjögren's syndrome and lupus.
Primary biliary cholangitis.

steps.x: **E. Rheumatoid factor.** RF = most sensitive; anti-CCP = most specific.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis started methotrexate 3 months ago. Her rheumatologist wants a blood test to track her disease activity at each visit, alongside the joint count. Her rheumatoid factor was strongly positive at diagnosis.
questions.q: Which blood test is most useful for monitoring her disease activity?
questions.e: RF is a poor marker for monitoring disease activity; the inflammatory markers (CRP/ESR) are used, and CRP or ESR feed into the DAS28.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which blood test is most useful for monitoring her disease activity? It wants a test (or a test result). Decide which test, and why, before reading the options.

clues: track her disease activity at each visit
rheumatoid factor was strongly positive at diagnosis
steps.x: Activity changes week to week: you need an **acute phase marker**, not an antibody.

elim: Used for diagnosis and prognosis, not activity.
Not a marker of RA activity.
A poor marker for monitoring activity.
Used in gout.

steps.x: **C. CRP.** Monitor RA with CRP/ESR (part of DAS28), not RF.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman has 10 weeks of symmetrical swelling of her MCP and PIP joints and wrists with 2 hours of morning stiffness. A medical student asks the rheumatology registrar what is needed to make the diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis.
questions.q: Which is the gold standard for diagnosis?
questions.e: The gold standard for RA is a clinical diagnosis supported by serology (RF and anti-CCP).

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the gold standard for diagnosis? It wants a test (or a test result). Decide which test, and why, before reading the options.

clues: what is needed to make the diagnosis
steps.x: RA has no single test: **clinical picture + RF/anti-CCP**.

elim: Used for septic arthritis, not RA.
Sensitive for synovitis but not diagnostic on its own.
Not needed in routine practice.
Erosions are late; waiting for them delays treatment.

steps.x: **A. Clinical diagnosis plus serology.** RA diagnosis = clinical + serology.

questions.stem: A 54 year old woman has had untreated seropositive rheumatoid arthritis for 4 years, refusing treatment until now. Her MCP joints and wrists are swollen and tender, and she is stiff for 3 hours each morning. Her CRP is 42 mg/L. X-rays of both hands and feet are taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on her hand X-ray?
o: Juxta-articular erosions with joint space narrowing
Pencil-in-cup erosions at the DIP joints
questions.e: Juxta-articular erosions are the hallmark of RA, with joint space narrowing and soft tissue swelling; osteopenia comes first.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on her hand X-ray? It wants a test (or a test result). Decide which test, and why, before reading the options.

clues: untreated seropositive rheumatoid arthritis for 4 years
steps.x: 4 years of untreated seropositive RA: expect **erosions** by now.

elim: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition in pseudogout.
Osteoarthritis.
Psoriatic arthritis.
Gout.

steps.x: **B. Juxta-articular erosions with joint space narrowing.** RA X-ray: periarticular osteopenia (earliest), then juxta-articular erosions (hallmark).

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate is reviewed in clinic. She has 4 tender and 3 swollen joints, and her CRP is 18 mg/L. She rates her overall health as 50 out of 100 and is stiff for 45 minutes each morning. Her DAS28 is calculated. DAS28 result (see item resources).
questions.q: Which best describes her disease activity?
questions.e: DAS28 measures RA activity: below 2.6 remission, 2.6 to 3.2 low, 3.2 to 5.1 moderate, above 5.1 high.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which best describes her disease activity? It wants a test (or a test result). Decide which test, and why, before reading the options.
Read the DAS28 against the cut-offs: **2.6, 3.2, 5.1**.

elim: Needs a DAS28 above 5.1.
DAS28 below 2.6.
DAS28 is not used this way; it grades activity.

steps.x: **C. Moderate disease activity.** DAS28: <2.6 remission, 2.6–3.2 low, 3.2–5.1 moderate, >5.1 high.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine has 1 swollen joint and 1 tender joint. His CRP is 6 mg/L and he rates his global health as 20 out of 100. He is stiff for 15 minutes in the morning. His DAS28 is 2.9. He asks whether his arthritis is in remission.
questions.q: Which best describes his disease activity?
questions.e: A DAS28 of 2.6 to 3.2 is low disease activity; remission needs a DAS28 below 2.6.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which best describes his disease activity? It wants a test (or a test result). Decide which test, and why, before reading the options.

clues: whether his arthritis is in remission
steps.x: 2.9 sits **between 2.6 and 3.2**.

elim: Needs a DAS28 above 5.1.
Needs a DAS28 below 2.6; his is 2.9.
He is close to target; this is not failure.

steps.x: **B. Low disease activity.** Remission is DAS28 below 2.6; 2.6 to 3.2 is low activity.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has a DAS28 of 5.8 despite methotrexate and sulfasalazine. Her rheumatologist plans to start adalimumab. She was born in India and moved to the UK at age 20. She has no cough or weight loss.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation before starting treatment?
o: Chest X-ray and interferon-gamma release assay (Quantiferon)
questions.e: TNF inhibitors can reactivate latent TB, so screen for latent or active TB (chest X-ray and Quantiferon) first.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation before starting treatment? It wants a test (or a test result). Decide which test, and why, before reading the options.
**TNF inhibitor** planned + born in a **high TB prevalence** country: screen for TB first.

elim: Already part of diagnosis; it does not change biologic safety.
Not required before a TNF inhibitor.
Not routinely needed before a TNF inhibitor.
Irrelevant to RA treatment.

steps.x: **B. Chest X-ray and interferon-gamma release assay (Quantiferon).** Before any TNF inhibitor: chest X-ray + Quantiferon for TB.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate still has a DAS28 of 3.9. Her rheumatologist plans to add hydroxychloroquine as a second conventional DMARD. She has no visual symptoms and her full blood count and liver tests are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation before starting hydroxychloroquine?
questions.e: Hydroxychloroquine can cause bull's eye retinopathy, so a baseline ophthalmology assessment and annual eye screening are needed.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation before starting hydroxychloroquine? It wants a test (or a test result). Decide which test, and why, before reading the options.
Hydroxychloroquine's key toxicity is the **retina**.

elim: Not needed for hydroxychloroquine.
Needed before biologics (TB screening), not hydroxychloroquine.
Not routine before hydroxychloroquine.
Sometimes done before methotrexate, not hydroxychloroquine.

steps.x: **B. Baseline ophthalmology assessment.** Hydroxychloroquine: baseline eye check, then annual screening (bull's eye retinopathy).

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has 3 months of symmetrical small joint pain in both hands with morning stiffness of 75 minutes. Her rheumatologist explains her blood results and says they are encouraging for her long-term outlook. Her CRP is mildly raised.
questions.q: Which result is most likely to have been described as encouraging?
o: Negative rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies
Positive rheumatoid factor at high titre
questions.e: A negative RF and low or absent anti-CCP are associated with a good prognosis in RA.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which result is most likely to have been described as encouraging? It wants a test (or a test result). Decide which test, and why, before reading the options.
Good prognosis is the **opposite** of the poor prognosis markers (RF, anti-CCP, HLA-DR4).

elim: Linked to erosions and a poor prognosis.
A poor prognostic factor.
A poor prognostic marker.
Reflects active inflammation, not a good outlook.

steps.x: **B. Negative rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies.** Negative RF and anti-CCP = better prognosis.

questions.stem: A 43 year old woman has had persistent symmetrical synovitis of her MCP joints and wrists for 7 weeks, with 2 hours of morning stiffness. Her anti-CCP is positive and CRP 28 mg/L. Hand X-rays show no erosions. She would rather wait and see whether it settles.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice about treatment?
o: Delay DMARDs until erosions appear on X-ray
Start a DMARD now, ideally within 3 months of symptom onset
Treat with NSAIDs alone for 12 months
Use long-term oral prednisolone instead of a DMARD
Wait 6 months to see if it resolves
questions.e: DMARDs (methotrexate first-line) should ideally start within 3 months of onset of persistent symptoms to prevent erosions.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate advice about treatment? It wants an action. Decide what you would actually do next before reading the options.
Persistent synovitis + **anti-CCP positive**: there is a **window of opportunity** to prevent erosions.

elim: Erosions are irreversible; the aim is to prevent them.
NSAIDs relieve symptoms but do not stop joint damage.
Delay beyond 3 months worsens outcomes.
Steroids are only a short bridge.

steps.x: **B. Start a DMARD now, ideally within 3 months of symptom onset.** Start a DMARD within 3 months of persistent RA symptoms.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man is newly diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis. His eGFR is 88 mL/min and his liver tests are normal. His rheumatologist starts methotrexate with a short course of prednisolone and folic acid, and the pharmacist checks the prescription carefully.
questions.q: Which is the correct way to take methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis?
questions.e: Methotrexate in RA is a once-weekly oral DMARD; daily dosing is a dangerous error.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the correct way to take methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis? It wants an action. Decide what you would actually do next before reading the options.
Methotrexate for RA is given on **one day a week**. Mistaken daily dosing kills.

elim: Not the RA regimen.
Daily dosing causes fatal toxicity; this is a classic prescribing error.
Far too often; risks marrow suppression.
Not the standard regimen.

steps.x: **C. Orally once a week.** Methotrexate = weekly, with folic acid on a different day.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman started weekly methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis 2 months ago. She now has painful mouth ulcers. Her haemoglobin is 112 g/L with an MCV of 104 fL. She has not been taking the second tablet she was prescribed. Her liver tests are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Folic acid is given with methotrexate to reduce side effects such as macrocytic anaemia and mouth ulcers.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? It wants an action. Decide what you would actually do next before reading the options.

clues: not been taking the second tablet
steps.x: Methotrexate + **mouth ulcers + macrocytosis** + missed second tablet = no **folic acid**.

elim: Does not treat methotrexate side effects.
The anaemia is macrocytic, not iron deficient.
Does not treat mouth ulcers caused by folate antagonism.
Dangerous; it would worsen toxicity.

steps.x: **C. Start folic acid supplementation.** Always co-prescribe folic acid with methotrexate.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has taken methotrexate at a full dose for 6 months. She still has 5 swollen joints and her DAS28 is 4.4. She has not had a biologic. Her liver tests and blood count are normal.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Continue methotrexate alone and review in 1 year
questions.e: If methotrexate monotherapy fails to achieve remission, NICE recommends adding another conventional DMARD (leflunomide, sulfasalazine or hydroxychloroquine).

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? It wants an action. Decide what you would actually do next before reading the options.

clues: methotrexate at a full dose for 6 months
steps.x: Monotherapy has **failed** (DAS28 4.4) and no biologic yet: **step up with a second conventional DMARD**.

elim: A gout treatment.
She is not at target; treatment must be escalated.
Steroid side effects outweigh benefit long term.
Biologics come after combination conventional DMARDs fail.

steps.x: **B. Add hydroxychloroquine or sulfasalazine.** NICE: methotrexate alone, then combination DMARDs, then biologics.

questions.stem: A 53 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is starting leflunomide because methotrexate caused persistent nausea. She has no other medical problems and is not planning a pregnancy. Her BP is 128/80 mmHg and her liver tests and blood count are normal. The rheumatology nurse plans her monitoring.
questions.q: Which additional monitoring is most important with leflunomide?
